title: How does a ballpoint pen work?

sources.name: National Inventors Hall of Fame — László Bíró and the modern ballpoint pen
BIC — Cristal 75th anniversary press kit: Engineering in miniature (pages 10–11)

practice: Try General Knowledge for more questions about familiar things and surprising ideas.

sections.html:
A ballpoint pen writes by rolling ink onto the paper. Its tiny metal ball turns inside a holder called a socket. Behind it, the reservoir stores the ink.

As the ball rolls, its surface picks up ink and transfers it to the page. Your apparently fixed pen tip has a moving part.
sections.title: The point is a moving part

sections.html:
Journalist László Bíró noticed that newspaper ink dried quickly, but it was too thick for a fountain-pen tip. The National Inventors Hall of Fame credits him with developing the modern ballpoint design.

The solution needed both suitable ink and a different way to deliver it.
sections.title: Better ink needed a different way out

sections.html:
BIC’s Cristal anniversary press kit describes a one-millimetre tungsten carbide ball, checked for roundness and resistance.

That measurement is the distance across the ball, not the width of its ink line. Other pens can use different sizes or materials.
sections.title: A tiny component has a demanding job

sections.html:
Picture ink, a turning ball and a line on paper. Which part must carry the ink between the other two?

Show the moving part

The ball’s surface. The reservoir stores ink; the socket holds the turning ball in place.

sections.title: Can you sketch the ink’s journey?

description: A ballpoint pen does more than let ink out of a tube. Its rolling tip transfers ink to the page—and helped solve a problem with thicker ink.
